United States Air Force

-Officers and enlisted personnel
The United States Air Force (USAF) divides

personnel into enlisted ranks and officer ranks. The

enlisted ranks are further divided into Airmen and

Non-commissioned Officers – the Air Force's mid

level supervisors. All NCOs are promoted from

junior enlisted ranks. The first level of NCO rank is
Staff Sergeant and promotion to this rank, as well as
further promotion, is based on a recommendation
from an airman's commander plus points awarded
for time in service, time in grade, performance
reports, decorations and the results of examinations.

Commissioned officers provide management and
leadership in their area of responsibility. Officers

hold the highest ranks in the military and they

receive their commission from the President. Every

year, the Air Force selects a number of enlisted
members for officer training but most officers come

from the Air Force Academy or from a civilian
university. In a similar way to NCOs, the promotion

of officers depends on merit.

Commissioned officers outrank all enlisted

personnel and even a recently commissioned second
lieutenant officially outranks the Chief Master

Sergeant of the Air Force. However, in practise
junior officers normally only exercise authority over

direct subordinates in their chain of command. For

Assignment abroad

10

example, because the squadron first sergeant

reports directly to the squadron commander, a

lieutenant would not normally give orders to this

NCO.

Enlisted personnel salute all commissioned

officers and commissioned officers salute their

superiors. The salute is a sign of respect towards the

officer's commission and is generally accompanied
by a polite greeting. The officer returns the salute

and willgenerally offer a similar greeting. Enlisted

personnel do not normally salute each other.

The Air Force has strict rules about the conduct of

officers and enlisted members. Close personal
relationships and business relationships between
officers and enlisted members are prohibited. These

relations are known as fraternization and the

penalties for officers can be severe, including court

martial and separation from the service.

When political and military leaders ask What sort of an army will
we need for the 21st Century?, the most common answer is A fully

professional army. Regular armies may be a good solution for large

rich countries. However, this solution is not always the best for

Smaller nations,especially countries with a developing economy.

The first problem is cultural and social. Although a number of countries have a long tradition of voluntary service. in

some societies the idea of a professional mercenary army is not widely accepted. A second problem is cost. Although

there may be a high social cost of taking a young man out of education or work, conscript soldiers are quite cheap. The
conscript accepts a lower standard of living, he is unaccompanied by his family and he needs litle support. The regular
soldier, by comparison, is expensive. He must be paid at rates similar to the commercial world and be provided with
housing and other social support. Although, a country might be capable of supporting a very large conscription-based
army, it might only be able to aford a very small regular force. For many countries, this willhave important

Consequences for their national defence.

A further problem has to do with readiness and small unit cohesion. Since they get little leave, conscripts are always
available for service. Regular soldiers, however, require longer leave periods and will frequently be away, either on leave
or on trainingcourses. addition, many conscript-based militaries use unit rotation and replacement which results in
high readiness and unit cohesion once units are formed and fully trained. Many regular professional militaries, on the
other hand, employ individual rotation and replacement. This system means a continuousS movement of personnel into
andout of units and can reduce smallunit cohesion and affect readiness. In addition, many professional forces have

The Law of Armed Conflict (LOAC)
LEGITIMATE TARGETS

Whether or not they wear a uniform, all persons directly participating in military operations

are combatants. Combatants are proper targets and can be attacked. All other persons,

including
civilians, medical personnel, chaplains, prisoners of war and enemy wounded, are
considered non-combatants. Non-combatants carnnot be directly targeted unless they engage in

hostile acts.

Military forces have an obligation to distinguish between civilians and military targets - this

is called the principle of distinction. The direct targeting of civilians is a breach of the LOẠC.
Similarly, attacks on civilian property and protected buildings (schools, religious buildings and

museums) are prohibited unless those buildings are being used for military purposes. The
LOAC expressly prohibits the use of protected buildings for military purposes.

Problems arise where military targets are located close to or within centres of population.

Attacks on these targets, even if they are expected to cause civilian deaths and other collateral
damage, are not strictly unlawful. However, in such cases military planners must also take into

account the principle of proportionality - attacks causing collateral damage are justified only if

the expected military advantage is far greater than the expected damage to the civilian

population. In any event, the LOAC prohibits area bombardment and other indiscriminate

attacks which do not distinguish between military objectives and civilian targets.

It is unlawful to attack medical personnel, facilities and vehicles provided they are properly

marked with a redcross or red crescent. Medical personnel may carry weapons as long as they

are used only to defend a medical facility against unlawful attack. Note that it is a serious

breach of the LOAC to store weapons together with medical supplies or to place combat assets

in a medical facility or vehicle.
It is also unlawful to pretend that you cannot be attacked under the laws of war. Such

abuses of the LOAC include using false markings on military aircraft, opening fire after you

pretend to surrender or pretending you are a civilian.

JOURNAL OF

COUNTER-TERRORISM

22 SPECIAL AIR SERVICE REGIMENT is the principal special
forces organisation of the British armed forces. The Regiment is
thought to number 400 troopers, although in 2004 UK Ministry
of Defence (MOD) announced that these numbers were to be
increased by approximately 20 percent.

The Regiment was formed during World War 2 by Lt David
Strling, a Scots Guards officer who had the idea of training a
small, highly-mobile force that would be able to operate
independently and strike fast behind enemy lines. Stirling's
original concept — covert military operations in denied areas —
continues to be a fundamental mission of the Regiment.
However, since the British Army deployed to Northern Ireland in the 1960s, the SAS have been increasingly
involved in Military Aid to Civil Power (MACP). MACP is assistance provided by the armed forces to the
police in maintaining law and order and is one of the fundamental tasks of the British Army. For 22 SAS,
MACP largely means counter-terrorism and hostage rescue — two tasks that the SAS Special Projects team
trains for continually. The UK is unusual in this respect since the use of military force in police functions is
forbidden by the laws of many countries such as the United States.

SAS personnel are frequently deployed abroad both for team tasks — training overseas special forces (SF)
operatives and on exercise with SF operatives from other countries. They are also sent to friendly countries
to give advice or as observers and it has been reported that at least one or two SAS personnel have been
present at every major counter-terrorism (CT) operation involving a friendly country in recent memory.
Although the SAS are considered to be one of the best CT units in the world, they have always been the first
to admit that they are continually looking for better ways of doing things.

United Nations Operation in Rafiki (UNOR)

BACKGROUND

Since the countries of Rafiki and Matata became independent in
1962, Matata has made repeated territorial claims on Odero,
Rafiki’s northern province. Matata has also provided logistics
and training support to the Odero Liberation Front (OLF) - an
insurgent group operating in the province. In December 2003,
rumours spread that large uranium deposits had been
discovered in Odero and civil war started in May 2004 when the
OLF launched attacks on government troops. The Matatan Armed
Forces invaded across the border in June 2004 after claiming
that Rafikian Armed Forces had illegally crossed the border in
pursuit of OLF fighters. Matatan forces captured Oderoville and
began killing the Ndulu ethnic minority.

While international pressure mounted, the warring factions
met in Cairo in September 2004 and agreed to an interim
ceasefire. This was followed in November by a comprehensive
peace agreement — the Cairo Agreement - which called for the
withdrawal of Matatan troops across the border, the
redeployment of Rafikian troops to positions occupied before the
outbreak of hostilities, free and fair elections in Odero and the
establishment of a UN peacekeeping force in the province. On 4
January 2005, the United Nations Security Council, acting under
Chapter VI of the UN Charter, authorised the deployment of the
United Nations Operation in Rafiki (UNOR) for an initial period of
six months. The Operation’s mandate included the use of all
necessary means to ensure respect for the ceasefire agreements,
disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) of former
combatants, the creation of the necessary security conditions for
the provision of humanitarian assistance and for the voluntary
return of refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs), and
assisting with the electoral process.

Four Generations of Warfare

The age of modern warfare, at least in Europe, began around
the middle of the 17th century. Up until this period, wars were
waged by families, tribes, religious groups, cities and even
businesses. The Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 brought about the
end of this period and from this time, the state had complete
control on war and the way war was fought. Many analysts
have called the period from 1648 to 1850 the first generation of
modern warfare or 1GW. This first generation was
characterised by massed manpower on the battlefield: cavalry
charges, bayonet charges, massed fires and line and column
tactics where troops stood shoulder-to-shoulder in densely
packed formations. In turn, this highly ordered battlefield led
to a military culture of order characterised by drill and
ceremonial, uniforms, saluting and rigid rank structures.
Second generation warfare (2GW) was largely brought
about by developments in firepower, communications and
transport. New technologies, like barbed wire and the
machinegun, greatly increased the destructive power
employed on the battlefield with the result that the old line and
column tactics became suicidal. Thus, the aim in war became

you for being here. I promised a few days ago

operation began in the early morning hours of
24 February. The coalition plan was for an
attack along the border by the Marines and
Arab coalition forces while the VII Corps and
XVIII Airborne Corps swept around to the
west of the enemy’s defences to envelop them,
sever their lines of communication, and isolate
and defeat their armor-heavy divisions.

the Ist Marine Division and the 2nd Marine
Division, with Arab Coalition forces launched
attacks over here on the right flank, in the
east, penetrating the enemy defensive belt and
breaching their tank obstacles.

At the same time, on the left flank in the west,
the French Daguet Division — that’s the 6th
French Light Armored Division with a
brigade of the 82nd Airborne Division,
attacked to secure Objective White and protect
the coalition’s west flank.

decided to begin the main effort 14 hours
early. At approximately 0530, the 1st Infantry
Division, moved forward and neutralized the
enemy’s defensive lines along the border. The
1st Armoured Division then went on to attack
through the breach to defeat enemy tactical
reserves and secure the corp’s eastern flank.

We were held up a little bit by the weather,
but by 8 o'clock in the morning, the 101st
Airborne launched an air assault deep into
enemy territory to establish forward operating
base COBRA at this location right here.

Tasks 1 & 2 [23]

The first phase in SAS selection is
known as the Special Forces Briefing
Course. This short course lasts a
weekend and over the course of these
two days, potential candidates are
shown what life in special forces is like
and are briefed on what to expect
during selection.

Those who decide to continue now
move on to the Endurance Phase - also
known as the Hill Phase. This phase
focuses on fitness and navigation. It
lasts four weeks and is held in the
Brecon Beacons and Elan Valley in
Wales. The Endurance Phase is
probably the hardest part of SAS
selection and training and about 90% of
candidates will drop out or be returned
to unit during these four weeks. The
first week mostly consists of runs up
and down hills with a small load in the
soldiers’ Bergen. As the weeks go by,
the load in the Bergen gets heavier and
heavier, the routes get longer and
longer and the navigation exercises
become more challenging. The final
week ends with the ‘Long Drag’ —
about 60 kilometres over difficult
mountain terrain and in less than 24
hours.

Of the 100 or so candidates who start
the Endurance Phase, only about ten
will be left at the end of the four weeks.
These candidates now move on to the
four-week Initial Continuation
Training, which consists of weapons
training with small arms, demolitions
and small patrol tactics. Those who are
not already parachute qualified, will
also complete the SAS parachute
training course during this phase.

After Initial Continuation Training,
candidates move on to the six-week
Jungle Training Course. This course
takes place in the jungles of Brunei and
soldiers will learn to live, fight and
survive in the jungle.

The last phase of training is Combat
Survival. Lasting four weeks, Combat
Survival is a month of training in
survival skills, living off the land and
using escape and evasion tactics. There
are lessons and lectures in resisting
interrogation and the Combat Survival
Phase ends with an escape and evasion
exercise. In groups, the soldiers have to
evade capture from the Hunter Force,
which is usually comprised of

has to resist tactical questioning. Even
at this last stage, if soldiers break and
give more information than their name,
rank, serial number and date of birth,
